descricao: Family member vocabulary, prefixes (step-, half-, great-, in-law), types of families, and relationship words.

secoes.conteudo:
Family vocabulary is some of the first English anyone learns. Mother, father, brother, sister — these are A1 words. But real conversations go much further. How do you say 'sobrinha'? What about 'cunhado'? Or 'enteado'? English has all of these, and they follow patterns that make them easy to learn once you see the logic.

Let's start with the core words. Your **parents** are your mother and father together. Your **siblings** are your brothers and sisters — **sibling** is the gender-neutral word that covers both, and it is very useful. 'Do you have any siblings?' is one of the most common conversation questions in English.

Your parents' parents are your **grandparents** — your **grandfather** and **grandmother**, often shortened to **grandpa** and **grandma** in informal English. Your **uncle** is your parent's brother, and your **aunt** is your parent's sister. Their children are your **cousins** — and in English, unlike in Portuguese, there is no different word for male or female cousins. Everyone is just a **cousin**. Simple.

Your own children are your **son** (male) and **daughter** (female). And here is an important pair to memorize together: your brother's or sister's children are your **nephews** (male) and **nieces** (female). **Nephew and niece** — they go together. If you remember one, remember the other.

secoes.titulo: Building New Words: Great-, In-Law, Step-, Half-
secoes.conteudo:
Here is where English family vocabulary gets really elegant. Instead of inventing completely new words for every relationship, English uses four simple prefixes that you can combine with words you already know. Once you learn the prefixes, you understand dozens of new words instantly.

The first prefix: **great-**. This means one generation further back than expected. Your **grandparents** are one generation above your parents. Add **great-** and you go one step further: your **great-grandparents** are your grandparents' parents. Their siblings are your **great-uncles** and **great-aunts**. Simple rule: every time you add **great-**, you go back one more generation.

The second prefix: **in-law**. This means family through marriage — not through blood, but through your husband or wife. Your partner's parents become your **in-laws** — specifically your **father-in-law** and **mother-in-law**. Their siblings become your **brother-in-law** and **sister-in-law**. When someone says 'my in-laws are visiting this weekend,' they almost always mean their partner's parents.

The third prefix: **step-**. This describes family through a parent's new marriage, not through blood. If your mother marries a new man, he becomes your **stepfather**. If your father remarries, his new wife is your **stepmother**. Their children from before the marriage become your **stepbrothers** and **stepsisters**. The step- relationship is legal and family — but not biological.

The fourth prefix: **half-**. This means sharing only one birth parent. A **half-sister** is the daughter of only one of your birth parents. For example, your father had a daughter with another woman before meeting your mother — she is your half-sister. You share a father but have different mothers. The **half-** relationship is biological but partial.

English has specific terms for different family structures. These words come up in conversation, in news articles, in films — and knowing them helps you understand discussions about modern life.

An **immediate family** is the small, close circle around you — usually just parents and children, sometimes including siblings. When someone says 'only immediate family is invited,' they mean a very small group. An **extended family** is the bigger picture — grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, everyone. When the whole **extended family** gets together for a holiday, it is usually a big, noisy gathering.

A **nuclear family** is a specific structure: two parents living together with their children, the traditional household. The image that comes to mind is mom, dad, and two or three kids under one roof. In modern societies, this is one of many possible structures — not the only one.

A **blended family** is increasingly common. It forms when two people come together in a new relationship and bring children from previous relationships. So you might have your children, your new partner's children, and then perhaps children you have together — all living as one family. The word **blended** is a good one: it suggests mixing things together into something new.

One more term worth knowing: **single parent**. A **single parent** is someone who has children but no partner living with them. They are raising their children alone — or perhaps with the help of extended family. It is a neutral, respectful term that describes a very common reality.

Beyond the names for family members, English has a rich vocabulary for the events and states that define family life. These words come up constantly in conversation.

Let's go in order of a typical relationship timeline. Two people start dating, then they decide to get **engaged** — they make a formal promise to marry. An **engagement** is the period between this promise and the wedding. You say 'they are engaged' or 'she got engaged last month.' Then they get **married** — they become legal partners in a wedding ceremony. After the wedding, they are a **married couple**.

Not all marriages last forever. When a marriage ends legally, the couple gets **divorced**. You say 'they are divorced' or 'my parents got divorced when I was ten.' **Divorce** is the legal process; **divorced** is the resulting state.

Now, some important vocabulary for modern relationships. A **partner** is anyone you are in a committed relationship with — husband, wife, boyfriend, or girlfriend. It is a useful word because it does not reveal the gender of the person, and it works for any kind of couple. 'My partner works in finance' tells you someone is in a relationship — nothing more.

**Relatives** are your family members — anyone connected to you by blood or marriage. **In-laws**, as we saw, are the family of your husband or wife specifically.

Two more useful words. **Raised** is the past tense of **raise**, meaning brought up as a child. 'She was raised by her grandmother' means her grandmother was the one who took care of her as she grew up. And **twin** — one of two children born to the same mother at the same time. **Identical twins** look exactly the same. **Fraternal twins** are born together but look different.

A few things in this topic are worth looking at carefully — either because they are false friends, or because they work differently from what you might expect.

The most important one: **relatives**. In Portuguese, 'relativos' usually means 'relative' in a philosophical sense — 'that's relative,' meaning it depends on the context. In English, **relatives** almost always means family members. 'I have a lot of relatives' = I have a big family. If you want to say something is 'relative' in the sense of 'it depends,' you say **relatively** (the adverb) or you use a phrase like 'it depends.' But as a noun, **relatives** = family members, almost every time.

Another one: **engaged**. In a relationship context, **engaged** means formally agreed to marry — as we saw. But **engaged** has other meanings in English that can be confusing. You can be 'engaged in' an activity — actively involved in it ('She is engaged in a project'). In British English, if you call someone and their line is busy, it is 'engaged' ('Sorry, the line is engaged'). And a person can be described as 'engaging,' meaning interesting and easy to like — very different from 'soon to be married.' Context always tells you which meaning is being used.

And one more: **mum** versus **mom**. Both mean mother — but **mum** is British English and **mom** is American English. You will see and hear both. Neither is wrong — it just shows where the speaker is from. The same goes for some other family words: British English often says 'mum' and 'dad,' while American English tends to say 'mom' and 'dad.' The actual family relationships are exactly the same.

Finally, a pattern worth noticing: the **-in-law** suffix always follows the family member title. It is always **mother-in-law**, never 'in-law mother.' The order is fixed. And the plural is **mothers-in-law**, not 'mother-in-laws' — though in informal speech, you will hear both, and nobody will judge you for it.
